newsitem.title: USA: U.S. new home sales finally hurt by rates in Oct.
newsitem.headline: U.S. new home sales finally hurt by rates in Oct.

text.p: An overdue correction in U.S. new home sales finally occurred in October, bringing the data in line with other soft housing sector indicators and confirming higher mortgage rates are biting into economic growth, economists said on Tuesday.

"It looks as if the rising rate environment finally took its toll on the housing industry with back-to-back substantial declines for new homes sales, if you include the big downward revision to September," said Kevin Flanagan, money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds.
Following a drop in U.S. housing starts in October, new home sales were the only data series which continued to hold near its cyclical high, analysts said.
While economists were on the lookout for a drop in October new home sales, the 8.7 percent fall to an annual rate of 714,000 units exceeded the average Reuter poll forecast for a slip to 772,000.
Exaggerating the correction was a sharp downward revision to September's data to an annualized 782,000 unit rate from a prior reported 816,000 unit rate.

"I didn't think in one month we would see this kind of a fall, but everyone was looking for a small drop. It was a sharper drop than we were looking for," said Marilyn Schaja, money market economist at DLJ Securities Corp.

The weak 0.5 percent drop previously reported for September new home sales had caused analysts to scratch their heads, contemplating whether the sales were impervious to a climb in mortgage rates seen earlier this year, they said.
Economists said mortgage rates hovered roughly one percentage point higher in the summer months from levels seen at the end of last year.
The recent dip in mortgage rates over the past two months has yet to show up in housing indicators due to the standard lag between a change in rates and buying patterns, experts said.
But some experts are looking for a slight bounceback in November's new home sales report.
"I think the numbers may bounce back a bit next month, but we are definitely coming off the highs of earlier this year," Schaja said.

U.S. Treasuries embraced the new home sales downturn and gained roughly a quarter of a point on the news. At 1100 EST/1600 GMT, the 30-year long bond had risen 16/32 to 102-11/32 to yield 6.32 percent.

"To have a fair and objective analysis, you have to look at it the other way -- that a bond rally could reinvigorate these interest rate sensitive sectors such as housing as you move into 1997," Flanagan said.
